summary: Rules-clean, correctly sized and well gated: the two muse_spark_norm_residual_kernel rows are measured (23.0/20.5, 78.0/74.7, ~398/396 us) and the byte floors check out. But the proposed kernel is structurally the incumbent (one 8192-wide row per CTA, 512 threads), so the realistic win is a few us per boundary, concentrated at turn_1 and turn_4, and close to nothing at first_turn. Judge it only on the two replaced rows. The headline move (~0.2-0.4%) is far below the 1.5-2.5% drift floor.
justification: Floors verified: 12 B/elem x 8192 x T at 4.8 TB/s gives 15.4 us (T=753), 61.7 us (3012) and 335 us (16384). Master's profile fb1e52d2119d4175 matches the hypothesis's numbers exactly: turn_1 23.0/20.5 (22.1/20.5 full), turn_4 78.0/74.7 (77.1/74.9), first_turn 395.8-398.6 us per boundary. Expected directions (all faster, small) agree with TASK.md weights. Shape-level savings: turn_1 ~5-9 us of 1080-1420, turn_4 ~10-20 us of 3335-4938, first_turn ~0-40 us of 14-22 ms. Each load's gain is <=0.7%, so the geomean moves ~0.2-0.4%, which is unreadable on the headline (LESSONS: 1.5-2.5% drift per shape). Triton row times reproduce within ~1%, so the replaced rows are readable. Mechanism caveats: (1) At first_turn the JIT kernel already sustains ~4.04 TB/s effective, and H200 practical streaming is ~4.0-4.3 TB/s, so the stated 90%-of-4.8 (~365 us) target is optimistic. Expect 0-5% on those rows. (2) The first boundary is slower than the second at every T (23.0 vs 20.5, 78 vs 75) because attn_boundary reads data['stream'] from a cold L2 while the branch input is partly L2-resident after the GEMM. That residency is the same for both kernels, so it is not a lever for the new one. (3) Where is the turn_1 gap (67-75% of floor) actually spent? Probably wave quantization and tail: 753 one-row CTAs on 132 SMs at 1-2 CTAs/SM of 512 threads is ~3-6 waves, plus launch ramp. The proposed design copies that structure. WEAKEST LINK: nothing in the change differs structurally from the incumbent JIT kernel. The same grid (one row per program), the same thread count (16 warps = 512 threads) and the same whole-row-in-registers approach give no a-priori reason to beat a hand-written CUDA kernel. A further cost: each program reloads alpha, beta, (1+w_pre) and (1+post_ffn) as fp32 [8192], 96-128 KB of L2 reads per row, against 96 KB of DRAM traffic per row. The levers that could actually beat the incumbent are absent: several rows per program or a persistent grid, so the weight vectors load once into registers and the tail shrinks at T=753, and the num_warps 8/16 sweep with 1-2 CTAs/SM. Recommend the implementer add a ROWS_PER_PROGRAM (1, 2, 4) or persistent-grid option to the prepare-time sweep, at no extra run cost.
confounders: sglang-pipeline-parity: established both boundaries as SGLang's FusedPostNormResidualPreNorm with router_dtype=None/branch_dtype=bf16. The change replaces exactly those calls, and the prepare() parity check is against those same modules. That is the baseline being compared, not a confound.

experts-triton-w4a16-first-turn-blockt256 and experts-hybrid-marlin-turn-triton-first-turn: they change only the expert GEMM path. The unpooler GEMM still sits between the experts and ffn_boundary, so the branch tensor and its L2 residency are unchanged. Neither touches the stream or the attention boundary. No plausible interaction.
interference: No companion is warranted. The change is self-contained, and the result is read from the two replaced rows in this run's profile: muse_spark_norm_residual_kernel x2 disappears and _norm_residual_boundary_kernel x2 appears, per shape, against master's known numbers. Triton kernel times reproduce within ~1%, so a 2-5 us move per row is resolvable at turn_1 and turn_4. No landed hypothesis overlaps this launch sequence or numerical path, so an ab-revert would re-measure unrelated code. The JIT-kernel control is master itself (fb1e52d2119d4175). Checks are spent and runs go out as scored submits, so spending a second run on an expected ~0.3% headline is not justified. One requirement makes the single run interpretable: prepare() must print which path it chose (Triton or the fallback to master's modules) and the chosen num_warps (and ROWS_PER_PROGRAM if added). The profile kernel names also show it, but a silent fallback would otherwise read as a null result.
rules_flags: None blocking. alpha/beta and the (1+w) effective weights are fp32 vectors derived from bf16 weights in prepare(). SGLang's own modules precompute exactly these (precompute_coefficients, precompute_effective_weight), so this is parity, not a precision change. Take them from the modules as specified, not re-derived.
The bf16 output (next_attn_input/ffn_input) stays bf16 and the stream stays fp32, as in SGLang. Internal fp32 math is fine.

The Triton-vs-fallback choice and the num_warps pick must happen in prepare() (shape/state only), never on input values inside kernel_fn. torch.empty outputs inside the captured graph are fine. There must be no synchronize, .item() or timing calls in kernel_fn: the graph-replay timing sweep belongs in prepare() only.
Bookkeeping: 'Built on master (635cfee)' names the submission blob. The master commit is b92a0f4719 (BEST.json). Base on b92a0f4.
open_questions: The bf16 max-ulp <= 1 parity gate on synthetic T=753 inputs: a different reduction order can flip the rounding of a few elements by 1 ulp. If any row's sum-of-squares ordering yields a 2-ulp difference, the gate silently falls back to master, which is a wasted scored submit. Consider gating on max ulp <= 2 plus a rel-L2 bound (e.g. <= 1e-5) on the bf16 output, and print the observed max ulp and rel L2 in the log.

Does the JIT kernel compute the post-norm of the branch fully in fp32, or round any intermediate (e.g. the normalized branch) to bf16 before the residual combine? The stream rel-L2 <= 1e-6 gate would catch a mismatch (bf16 rounding gives ~1e-3 on the beta*b term), but only after the change was built. Check the JIT source (sglang muse_spark_v12/fused_norm_residual) first.

MuseSpark1xRMSNormWithInputScale with is_post_norm=True and post_norm_gain_center_type='one': confirm that the input scale (1+post_ffn) is the only weight applied, and that there is no post-normalization gain. The hypothesis asserts this, and the parity check will catch it if it is wrong.

Would multi-row programs (2-4 rows per CTA, weights loaded once) or a persistent grid be the actual win at T=753? If the single-row variant lands within 1 us of the JIT kernel at turn_1, that is the next stacked hypothesis.
